raw_case_text:
A male in his 40s, who had been diagnosed with HIV 6 years previously, presented with a 7-month history of disseminated nodular and ulcerating lesions (Figs 1 and 2). Verbal informed consent was obtained from the patient. However, because the patient was lost to follow-up and attempts to contact him or his family has been unsuccessful, written consent could not be obtained. No patient-identifying details are included in this paper. The lesions worsened in the month prior to presentation and became predominantly ulcerative, with partial loss of the nose. The lesions were multiple, well-circumscribed, round to oval, hyper-pigmented ulcers with elevated borders ranging in size from 2-6 mm. The lesions were located on the face, scalp, chest, back, and upper and lower limbs. The patient reported associated generalized body pains, fatigue, night sweats, loss of appetite, loss of weight and a productive cough. Various antibiotics alone or in combinations were used without success. The patient also confessed to poor adherence to his antiretroviral therapy (ART), which consisted of abacavir, lamivudine and lopinavir/ritonavir. His HIV viral load was 149, 455 copies ml-1, and his CD4 count was 34 cells mm-3 at the time of presentation. He previously had pulmonary tuberculosis in 2009 and in 2017, which was treated successfully.
Chest X-ray showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. Investigations for syphilis showed a positive   Treponema pallidum   haemagglutination (TPHA) test result and a non-reactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test. Other investigations included a serum cryptococcal antigen test, which was negative, a blood culture, which showed growth of   Staphylococcus hominis  , and a tuberculosis (TB) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (Xpert MTB/Rif Ultra; Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) test performed on sputum, which did not detect   Mycobacterium tuberculosis   complex. Multiple skin punch biopsies from the left and right cheeks, right elbow, right chest and back were taken and submitted for mycological culture and histological examination. Sputum samples were also collected and submitted for mycological, mycobacterial and general bacterial cultures. Sputum and tissue microscopy revealed no acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Mycological culture of tissues and sputum revealed colonies at 25  C that were slow growing, moist and glabrous, with a wrinkled and folded surface. Colonies were white with an orange-brown reverse (Figs 3 and 4). The lactophenol cotton blue stain showed solitary and erect conidiophores arising at right angles from thin septate hyphae that tapered toward the apex. Conidia were formed in clusters on tiny denticles at the apex of the conidiophore, with their arrangement being suggestive of a flower (Fig. 5). Conidia were ovoid, hyaline, one-celled and smooth-walled. On blood agar, incubated at 37  C, colonies were tiny, glabrous, white to greyish and yeast-like, and consisted of spherical or oval budding yeast cells on Gram stain microscopy.
The organism was identified as S. schenckii based on macroscopic and microscopic characteristics. The identification was confirmed by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (VITEK mass spectrometer, bioMerieux, Marcy I'Etoile, France). Histological examination showed variable epidermal ulceration, which was undermined by acute inflammation admixed with fibrin and granulation tissue. The dermis contained a dense chronic inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes and numerous giant cells. In addition, numerous small, round to oval, cigar-shaped fungal elements and asteroid bodies were observed. The subcutis was unremarkable. The periodic acid-Schiff-diastase (PAS-D), Alcian blue (AB), PAS and Grocott stains highlighted the fungal organisms. The Warthin-Starry stain showed no micro-organisms.   T. pallidum   immunostaining showed negative immunoreactivity.

subjective.chief_complaint: A male in his 40s presenting with a 7-month history of disseminated nodular and ulcerating skin lesions, productive cough, night sweats, and profound weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 7-month history of progressive disseminated nodular and ulcerative cutaneous eruptions that markedly worsened over the preceding month, resulting in extensive tissue destruction and partial loss of the nose. Lesions were associated with generalized body aches, fatigue, drenching night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, and productive cough. Multiple prior courses of single and combination antibacterial therapies yielded no clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Receiving antiretroviral therapy (abacavir, lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir) with reported suboptimal medication adherence; history of pulmonary tuberculosis in 2009 and 2017, both treated successfully to completion.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized body pains, fatigue, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, and productive cough; denies headache or visual changes.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: Multiple well-circumscribed, round-to-oval, hyperpigmented ulcers with elevated borders measuring 2-6 mm in diameter distributed across the face, scalp, chest, back, and upper and lower extremities, with extensive ulceration and partial tissue destruction of the nose.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiograph: Bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. Serology: Treponema pallidum hemagglutination (TPHA) test positive; rapid plasma reagin (RPR) non-reactive. Cryptococcal antigen: Serum cryptococcal antigen test negative. Sputum diagnostics: Sputum microscopy negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB); tuberculosis PCR (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Blood culture: Growth of Staphylococcus hominis.
objective.advanced_workup: Multiple skin punch biopsies (cheeks, right elbow, chest, and back) and sputum mycological workup: Sputum and tissue microscopy negative for acid-fast bacilli. Tissue histology demonstrated epidermal ulceration with dense chronic dermal infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes, and multinucleated giant cells) with numerous round-to-oval, cigar-shaped fungal elements and asteroid bodies highlighted by PAS-D, Alcian blue, PAS, and Grocott stains; Warthin-Starry stain and T. pallidum immunostaining were negative. Fungal cultures at 25 °C yielded slow-growing, moist, wrinkled white colonies with orange-brown reverse, showing flower-like clusters of conidia on conidiophores on lactophenol cotton blue stain; subculture at 37 °C yielded yeast-like colonies with spherical/oval budding yeasts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) with cutaneous and pulmonary involvement in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and severe immunosuppression (baseline CD4 count 34 cells/mm3, HIV viral load 149,455 copies/mL). Diagnostic confirmation: Definite identification of Sporothrix schenckii confirmed by characteristic macroscopic/microscopic fungal dimorphism and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS; VITEK MS). Secondary Treponema pallidum seropositivity (TPHA reactive, RPR non-reactive) representing treated or latent treponemal infection; blood culture isolate of Staphylococcus hominis consistent with skin flora/contaminant. Plan & Outcome: Patient was initiated on diagnostic evaluation and specialized mycological therapy, but was subsequently lost to outpatient follow-up.
